title: Intros and agenda
gist: Small talk about the Pacific Northwest and peak season, intros for Asher and Elena, and Tom sets a no-demo, discovery-only agenda.

turns.t: Hey, there he is. Marcus, how are you doing?
Hey Tom. Good, good. Sorry, I'm like two minutes late, I had a dispatcher grab me in the hallway on the way back from the yard. Classic Tuesday.
No, totally fine. That's kind of the whole reason we're talking, right? Dispatchers grabbing you in hallways.
Ha. Yeah. You're not wrong.
Is Elena joining? I saw she accepted the invite.
She is, she's — oh, there she is. Elena, I think you're on mute.
Sorry. Yes. Hi. I was in another call that ran over, I'm here now.

Hi Elena, nice to meet you. So I've got Asher on with me as well. Asher runs product at Tandem. I figured since you all have a pretty specific setup, it'd be good to have him on early instead of me playing telephone back to the product team.
Hey everyone. Yeah, happy to be here. I mostly want to listen today, honestly. Tom's driving.
Hey Asher. Where are you guys based? Are you down in the Bay?
Asher's in Oakland, I'm actually in Portland, so I'm basically your neighbor. How's the weather up there in — you're in Tacoma, right?

Kent. Close enough, nobody outside Washington knows the difference. It's doing that thing where it's sunny for an hour and then it's just not. Which, honestly, for us is fine. Fall's when volume ramps up and I would rather not have snow on top of that. Snoqualmie Pass in December is its own meeting.
Yeah, I bet. Peak season's coming. When does it really kick in for you?

Mid-October, and then it just doesn't stop until like the second week of January. The retail customers start pulling inventory forward, everybody wants their stuff in the DCs before Black Friday, and then there's returns after Christmas. So, yeah. Good timing for this conversation. Or terrible timing, depending on how you look at it.

Ha, we'll try to make it good timing. So here's what I was thinking for today, and stop me if you want to go somewhere else. Thirty-ish minutes. I'd love to just understand how dispatch works for you today, where it's breaking, what Elena's world looks like on the systems side, and then how you'd want to evaluate something like this. I'm not going to do a demo today, and that's on purpose. If it makes sense, we'll set up a proper one with our engineering folks on your data. Sound okay?
Yeah, that works. I appreciate not getting a forty-slide deck, honestly. The last vendor did twenty minutes on their founding story.
Works for me.

title: Dispatch today: spreadsheets, overtime and chargebacks
gist: Marcus describes nightly spreadsheet routing for 420 trucks, overtime at about 14% of driver hours against a 6% target, and roughly $40k/month in late-delivery chargebacks; success would be dispatchers home by seven, overtime under 8% and chargebacks halved.

turns.t: Great. So Marcus, maybe start wherever's easiest. Walk me through a night in dispatch.

Sure. So, okay, the short version is we run 420 trucks. Mostly regional freight, LTL and some full truckload, Washington, Oregon, a little bit of Idaho. We've got three terminals, Kent, Portland and Spokane. And every night the dispatch team builds the next day's routes. In spreadsheets. I wish I was exaggerating. It's Excel, it's a handful of really smart people who have been doing it for fifteen years, and a lot of tribal knowledge about which dock at which DC is going to make you wait two hours if you show up at 6:05 instead of 5:55.
Right. How many people are building routes?

Nine dispatchers across the three terminals, plus two leads. And they start around, I want to say four in the afternoon, once the order cutoff hits, and on a bad night they're there till ten, eleven. Which, you know, they're salaried, so that's not my overtime number, but it's a burnout number. I lost a lead in Spokane in June and it took me three months to backfill.
Wow. Okay.
Sorry, quick one. Roughly how many stops does a truck do in a day? Just so I have the shape of it in my head.

Depends on the terminal. Kent and Portland, the LTL trucks, eight to fourteen stops, a lot of them are DCs and some industrial. Spokane is longer hauls, fewer stops, more miles. If you averaged it out across the whole fleet, call it ten stops a truck. So something like four thousand stops a night, give or take, across the three terminals. On a peak day more.
Okay, got it. Thanks.

And the thing is, they're good. Like, the routes aren't terrible. But they're built for the plan, right? And the plan's dead by 7 a.m. A truck goes down, a driver calls out, a DC pushes an appointment, and then it's phones and whiteboards and somebody re-sorting a spreadsheet at a stoplight. Not literally. Hopefully.
When a truck goes down mid-day, what actually happens? Like, who re-plans, and how?

The lead at that terminal. Mostly by gut. They'll pull up Samsara, look at who's closest, and call around. Hey, can you pick up these four stops on your way back. And the driver says yes, because they're nice people and they want the hours, and then they blow through their day, and that's my overtime problem.
Yeah, let's talk about that. What's overtime looking like?
So, it's — I literally had this number up this morning. It's about fourteen percent of driver hours. Fourteen, fifteen. Let's say fourteen, I'll get yelled at by finance if I round up.
Fourteen percent of total driver hours is overtime.

Of total hours, yeah. And our target internally, the number we actually budget for, is six. So we're more than double. And some of that's peak, sure, but it was eleven in the spring. It's not just a seasonal thing, it's been creeping for a year and a half.
And that's paid at time and a half, I assume.

Time and a half, yeah. And then there's the hours-of-service piece, which is the scarier one. If a driver hits their limit, we've got a truck sitting at a truck stop somewhere with somebody else's freight on it and a relief driver two hours away. That's happened. Twice in August.
Three times.
Three times. Thank you. Elena keeps me honest. She has the Samsara logs, I have my memory.
Ha. Okay. And then on the customer side, you mentioned DCs. I'm guessing there are chargebacks?

Oh, yeah. That's the one that gets Dana's attention. So most of our big shippers, the retail ones, they run on-time-in-full programs. You miss your appointment window at the DC, they fine you. It's a percentage of the invoice or a flat fee depending on the retailer, and some of them are, honestly, pretty aggressive about it. There's one big-box account where fifteen minutes late is the same as not showing up. We're running about forty thousand a month in late-delivery chargebacks right now.
Forty thousand a month.

Give or take. Some months it's thirty-five. September was worse, I haven't seen the final yet. And that's money that just disappears. There's no fighting most of them, we've tried, the retailers have all the leverage.
Do you have a sense of how much of that is the plan being bad versus things going wrong during the day?

That's a great question and the honest answer is no, not really. My gut says it's like half and half. Some of it is we just build a route that was never going to make a 6 a.m. window at a DC, because the dispatcher forgot that dock is always backed up on Tuesdays, or they stacked too many stops before it. And some of it is the truck broke down at nine and nobody re-planned fast enough, so the 2 p.m. appointment at the other end of the route just quietly dies.
Okay. That's helpful. That split matters a lot for what we'd actually try to fix first. The nightly plan is the easier win, the mid-day re-plan is where it gets interesting.

So if I play that back. 420 trucks, three terminals, routes built manually every night in spreadsheets, overtime at fourteen percent of driver hours against a target of six, and about forty k a month in chargebacks. Plus the hours-of-service risk, which is more of a safety and compliance thing. Did I miss anything?
No, that's — when you say it out loud it's kind of bleak. There's one more, the customer calls, but let's park that. Elena's going to want to talk about systems before I get on my soapbox.
Ha. Fair. Let's park it, I wrote it down. What would good look like for you, though? Like, if we're sitting here in six months and this worked, what's different?

Honestly? Dispatchers go home at seven. Overtime under eight percent. Chargebacks cut in half, so call it twenty k a month instead of forty. If I could walk into Dana's office with that, I don't have to sell anything internally. It sells itself.
That's a really clear bar. I like that a lot. It's measurable, too, which makes my life easier. Have you tried to fix this before? Like, is there a routing tool that came and went?

Ha. Yes. So about four years ago, before my time actually, they bought a routing add-on that came bundled with the TMS. Oracle had a module. It ran overnight, it spat out routes, and the dispatchers looked at them and said these are garbage, and went back to Excel within like a month. And to be fair to the dispatchers, the routes were garbage. It didn't know anything about dock times, it didn't know a driver's hours, it just did shortest path. So there's a little bit of scar tissue on the floor. When I say routing software to my leads, the first face they make is not a happy face.
That's really good to know. So adoption with the dispatchers is its own thing we'd need to earn.
A hundred percent. If my Kent lead, Ray, doesn't buy in, it doesn't matter what I sign. He'll just quietly keep the spreadsheet open on his second monitor. I would, too, honestly, if I were him.

That's actually one of the things we designed around. Dispatchers can override anything the engine does, drag a stop, lock a route, and it'll re-plan around what they locked instead of fighting them. It's meant to feel like a really fast assistant, not an autopilot. But again, better to show than tell. Thursday or whenever we do the demo, it'd be great if Ray could be on.
Maybe. Let me see. He's not a big Zoom guy. But if I can get him to watch the recording, that might be enough.

title: Systems, integrations and security
gist: Elena lays out Samsara telematics, a heavily customized 2014 on-prem Oracle TMS with no API, and requirements for Okta SSO, a SOC 2 Type II report and a 180-question security questionnaire; Tom defers the deep integration question to Daniel.

turns.t: Elena, over to you. What does the landscape look like on your side?

Okay. So, telematics is Samsara. All 420 trucks have Samsara units, we've been on them about three years. That part is fine, it's modern, there's an API, we already pull GPS and hours of service from it into a couple of internal dashboards. The problem is the TMS. We're on Oracle Transportation Management, on-prem, and the version is from 2014. It's heavily customized. Nobody who customized it still works here.
Ah. The classic.

Yes. Very classic. So the orders live there. Customer appointments live there. Rates live there. And there is no real API. There are some database views that I'm allowed to read, and there's a batch export that runs every night for finance. That's it. Upgrading it is a separate project, and that project is not funded, so please don't tell me the answer is upgrade the TMS.
Ha, noted. Do the dispatchers export from the TMS into the spreadsheets today?
Yes. Every afternoon, the export lands on a shared drive, someone pastes it into the template. Sometimes the wrong day's file. That has also happened.
We don't talk about that week.

Okay, so, I won't pretend to be the right person for the deep integration question. That's exactly why I want Daniel on the next call. He's our staff engineer, he's built most of our integrations. But at a high level, we already have a Samsara integration, it's live with a number of our customers. And for the TMS side we've done file-based integrations before, so it's not a new problem for us.
Which customers on Oracle on-prem?

Uh, that's a — I'd want to check which ones are specifically Oracle. I know we've done older on-prem TMS setups, there's a parcel fleet in Ohio on some ancient system, I don't remember which one off the top of my head. I'll get you a straight answer on that instead of guessing.
Please. Because I have heard 'we've done file-based integrations' from three vendors now and every time it turns out to be a CSV upload button in the UI and a person whose job is to click it.

That's fair. And for what it's worth, there's a real difference between someone uploading a CSV once a day and a scheduled pull with validation and error handling and alerting when the file doesn't show up. Daniel can walk you through what it actually looks like. I'd rather he show you than we describe it.
Okay. Good. I'll also want to know what happens when an order changes in the TMS after the export. Because that happens constantly.
Yeah, that's a good one. Is the change rate high? Like, how many orders get modified after the nightly cutoff?
I don't have a precise number. Marcus?

Ten percent? Maybe more in peak. Appointment changes mostly. A DC calls and moves a slot, or a customer adds a pallet. The dispatchers find out by phone and then somebody updates the TMS later. Sometimes much later.

So the TMS is not always the source of truth, is what he's saying. Which is a problem for any integration, not just yours. I just want to be clear about it up front so nobody acts surprised in the pilot.
No, that's really helpful. And on the network side, can anything talk to that box from the outside, or is it locked down?

Locked down. Nothing inbound. We can push files outbound over SFTP, that's how we do the finance export to our accounting provider. Anything that needs a connection into the data center goes through a change board, and the change board meets once a month, and they are not fast people.

Got it. So outbound SFTP is possible today, inbound is a change board. That's a good thing for Daniel to know before Thursday, or, sorry, before the demo, whenever we land it. Okay. Writing all that down. What else is on your list? Security, SSO?

Yes. So, SSO is Okta. Anything new has to be behind Okta, no exceptions, our CISO is very clear about that. SAML is fine. SCIM for provisioning would be nice, it's not a hard requirement. Then security review. I'll need your SOC 2 report, Type II, and we have a security questionnaire. It's, I think, about 180 questions. I'm sorry in advance.
No, that's totally normal. We're SOC 2 Type II, I can get you the report under NDA this week. And the questionnaire, send it over, we have folks who turn those around.

And roles. We'd need at least three. Dispatchers, terminal leads, and a read-only role for customer service. We manage all of that in Okta groups, so I'd want the roles to come from the group, not be set by hand in your admin screen by whoever remembers to do it.

Yep, we map roles from SAML group claims, so that works the way you'd want. I'll double check on SCIM, I believe it's supported on the enterprise plan, but I'd rather confirm than say yes and be wrong.
Okay. And the questionnaire, how long does it usually take you?
Usually about a week, a week and a half for one that size.
Hm. Okay. If it's a week and a half that's fine. If it's a month, that's the decision date, so.
No, understood. We'll prioritize it. I'll make sure it doesn't become the long pole.
Okay. And data. Where is the data hosted, and does any of our customer data go to third parties? Like, are you sending our stops to some mapping provider?

We're hosted in AWS, US regions. We do use a third-party map data provider for the road network and traffic. Addresses and coordinates go to it for routing, no customer names, no order details. That'll all be in the questionnaire answers and the subprocessor list, but I want you to hear it now and not be surprised by it later.
Okay. I appreciate that. That's the kind of thing that usually comes up in week five.
Elena's killed two vendors in week five.
They deserved it.
Ha. Noted. We'll try very hard not to be the third.
